They are correct. Unfortunately there isn't much footage of Western Gun out on the internet; the game doesn't use a computer processor (it's TTL-based) and as such emulation is a giant pain that no one has really gone through the trouble to do yet. And being a game from the mid-70s, there's not much footage of an actual cabinet online either - that video is about the best I've come across. But it is true that Gun Fight is essentially a remake of the concept with a microprocessor and a different art style.

According to the book They Create Worlds, Jeff Frederiksen had been working on developing a pinball machine that used an Intel 4004 earlier in the 1970s before the idea got shelved (due to a lack of interest from manufacturers), but decided to improve on the system he had developed there to make a coin-op video game system that used an MPU - in this case, the 8080 microprocessor. He ended up developing the first bit-mapped display outside of computer research labs, got Dave Nutting to bring in Jamie Fenton and Tom McHugh, which led to the development of Amazing Maze (as a test program that eventually became a commercial release), and Gun Fight (by McHugh and Dave Nutting himself). Bally had recently licensed Western Gun but weren't a fan of the squished, cartoony visuals, so the microprocessor system was a good solution. It also allowed them to replace the fixed playfield from the original game with a stage that changes after each round.

Interestingly, the first five microprocessor-based games Dave Nutting Associates made for Bally-Midway would all end up being early Bally Arcade games - Amazing Maze, Gun Fight, 280 Zzzap, Sea Wolf, and Tornado Baseball!

I took a look at the screenshot for the incredibly-named "Death Maze 5000."  I'm familiar with "3D" games of that sort.

The Astrocade does have one kind of 3D "game."  But this is a stretch:

One of the game-playing aids for Rich Tietjens 1980 release, "Dungeons & Dragons" has a sub-program called, I think, "Dungeon Maker."  The Dungeon Master has a TV on the gameplay table along with his trusted Bally Arcade.  The BASIC program has a few menus asking for the details about the dungeon ahead of the players.  After the questions are answered, then a first-person, wire-frame view of the dungeon is created.  The DM turns the TV around and the players get to see what their character's face ahead of them.  This is a pretty neat idea.  I've tried it (not while playing D&D, sadly) and the final drawn dungeon works pretty good and is rather convincing.

Oh, and Lance's description of a game where the player's poor rat starts to hallucinate when it goes hungry?  That's odd.  It sounds like a clever gameplay variation idea.  Cheese, cheese everywhere and not a bite to eat!

Here's how I converted the plain text file with the code for Star Trek that Kevin sent to me to a WAV file using the 300-Baud tools.  I did the conversion using the 64-bit version of Windows 7. 

You'll need the following two programs for the conversion of a plain text file to a 300-Baud WAV file that can be downloaded into Bally BASIC:

1) txt2prg
2) KCS

Download and install the 300-baud tools from here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/tape_archive_tools/tape_archive_tools.html

These two programs must be run them from the command line.  Here's an overall sequence of what to do:

1) Place the two conversion programs in separate directories.
2) Move the Star Trek text file into the txt2prg folder.
3) Get to the Windows command prompt with CMD from the Run box
4) Navigate to the txt2prg folder and type:

txt2prg startrek.txt startrek.prg

5) After that's done, then move startrek.prg into the KCS folder.
6) Navigate to the KCS folder in the command Window and type:

kcswin -M -L5 -P50 startrek.prg

Now you'll have a file called STARTREK.WAV.  This file is about 4MB in size and about three minutes long.  It can be loaded into Bally BASIC using the 300-baud interface.

I've attached two screenshots of me running these two programs.  I hope that this helps.

If you need more help, then let me know.

There are multiple reasons that this program will not work in Bally Basic (300 baud). All of the   red spaces are NOT needed This will take up too much valuable space. There are only 1800 characters available for all program text AND the @() array spaces. Each @() space requires 2 bytes. If you check your SZ and you need 50 A() positions, you will need a SZ of 100 minimum (102 prefered).

Line 525 is not good programming. It says to print something and immediately it clears the screen and ends the program by going to the 700 last line of the program.

Are you still having any issues, Kevin? I didn't need to make any changes to run the utilities on Windows 10, but compatibility mode is definitely a good thing to try.

Indeed, you should try to avoid any unnecessary spaces (though spaces are needed after some keywords).

Adam already went through the basic workflow, but I'll also point out that the 300 baud program downloads should include .prg files. Some of the older ones have .txt files displayed in all caps like they would appear on the system itself, but really the editable format is more useful. If you want examples of editable text files, they're easy to create from the .prg files.

prg2txt.exe spacecheckers.prg spacechecker.txt -e -n

-e is for editable format, and -n displays non-character bytes in curly braces instead of just question marks like they'd appear when loading a program into Bally BASIC.

I pulled that .prg file from here, but there are lots available, some more complicated than others.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/l&m_software/Space%20Checkers%20(1981)(L&M%20Software)(300%20baud).zip

It would indeed be cool to type in programs where all we have is a scan of the source code. It's been awhile since any new tapes have showed up.

Michael Matte wrote to Datamax, Inc. in the 1980s and purchased the schematics and board layouts for the system.  He has had them since that time.  Michael based his hi-res Astrocade upon the schematics, so he did put them to good use.

The largest of these UV-1 drawings are 24" x 36".  We've been trying to figure out how to get scans of them for quite awhile.  He's taking a stab at it this week.  He has been reluctant to send the original drawings, as they could get lost in the mail.  However, he's decided to photocopy them as best as he can and then send me the originals so that they may be scanned locally.  This will probably be expensive, so I will ask here for donations to get this done.  We'll figure that out in the next month or two once I see what he sends my way.

Attached is a hand-written list that Michael sent to me that gives the details for the schematics and board layouts.  This includes schematics for such neat hardware as the interface for the floppy drive and the "Winchester drive" (yes, a hard drive!).  Also included are the schematics for the video, RGB and digitizer boards, plus other UV-1R goodies.

All of this is neat, but we still don't have access to the Z-GRASS ROM for the UV-1 system.  I guess there must be some sort of operating system too, which is included on a floppy disk, I think.  I wonder if it's some variation on CP/M?  I hope that someday a UV-1 computer pops up for sale and the software can be archived-- if it has survived after all these years.

Below is an email from Michael detailing his plans for the UV-1 drawings.

Adam

From: Michael Matte

I'm planning to work on my Datamax drawings project next week. For myself, I will visit the UPS store and break down each blueprint into four 11x17" scanned photocopies. Fortunately, the drawings don't utilize 100% of the larger 24x36" blueprints, so this scan idea will work.

Every 11x17" blueprint scanned photocopy will be labeled (by me) with:

Datamax board name

For example, the upper left Digitizer Board's schematic photocopy will be labeled as:

18047:
When I played the game I started in a quadrant that already had two Klingon ships, which was helpful enough. Once you're in the same space as the Klingons, you have to do a short range scan, which should alert you to their presence and give you a targeting trajectory. Then you go to "fire" and enter that number; it doesn't look like it always hits but it usually did for me. Movement is always unique in practically every version of the game I've played - some of them have you move by entering a radial direction and a number of sectors (or quadrants), some have you using positive and negative numbers to move horizontally and vertically, others just have you put in the coordinates you want to move to. Haven't quite figured out which one of these Waldinger's game is. His directions don't really make it clear - if anyone can suss it out looking at the code that would be welcome.
There are so many versions of Star Trek that it's hard for me to really say which this version was based off of originally. Typically you had around 64 quadrants consisting of 64 "sectors" within them for your galaxy map, though some versions had around 36 of each, etc.I'm not sure if the phasers in this version use the ship's energy supply like they do in others, nor do I know if they lose potency over distance - in versions with photon torpedoes, that is usually the alternative that you have to specifically aim at Klingon ships, and they always do full damage.
I think most versions of Trek on the Bally are based on some extent on the ones that either were printed in David Ahl's 101 Basic Computer Games book, or the one created for Palo Alto TinyBASIC (which Bally BASIC is based off of) and printed in People's Computer Company. I got the package of UV-1R information and schematics from Michael Matte two days ago.  Among many pieces of documentation are two original original flyers promoting the system.  I've taken 600dpi scans of the pictures on the flyer and attached them here.  These are the highest quality pictures of the UV-1R system that I've seen to date.  The second picture, with the UV-1R accessories, is the first time I've seen a complete UV-1R set-up.  Oh, and for those who are wondering, the "R" in UV-1R stands for Rackmount, as this is the system that is meant to go in a rack in a production studio.

For those who may not understand what they're looking at here, the UV-R1 computer in January 1983, cost $7,695.  It used the same three Bally custom chips used in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade; it ran in hi-res mode.  The UV-1R is just the stand-along system in the first picture.  Michael Matte included a revised price list from July 17, 1984 which shows the reduced price of the UV-1 to be $2,000 only six months later!  That's quite a decrease in the price of the system!

The second picture of the UV-1, shows the system with most of its accessories.  Here's what makes up the complete DATAMAX UV-1R Zgrass Graphics System (this information is taken directly from the flyer):

Basic Configuration:

* Graphics Tablet: the electronic canvas upon which an image can be drawn. Summagrahics Bit Pad One with power supply and four-button cursor.

* Video Monitor: Panasonic CT-1350 MG

* DATAMAX UV-1R Zgrass Graphics Computer: the heart of the system, contains the Zgrass language. Z80 microprocessor, 320 x 201 pixel resolution, 256 colors with four colors displayable per screen area.

* Computer Terminal: Televideo 910

* Floppy Disk Drive: for auxiliary storage. DATAMAX DFD-1 Dual 5.25" Floppy Drive with .77 Mbyte capacity.

* DATAMAX RGB Converter: for direct RGB output.

* Joystick Hand Controller: for special input purposes.

Software Options:

* Chart Package: for easy creation of bar, pie, and line charts with the excitement of animation.

* Weather Package: to create, edit and display animated weather maps.

* Plotter Package: Software interfaces for producing hardcopy plots.

* Fonts: nine additional available.

* Zgrass Swap Module Preparation Package: documentation and software for custom expansion of the Zgrass language.

* CP/M: makes accessible the extensive library of CP/M business and word-processing software.

* Custom software designed upon request.


Hardware Options:

* Printers: Okidata Microline 82A and Epson MX-80 Plus

* Plotters: HP7220C Graphic Plotter and HIPLOT Digital Plotter DMP Series


This computer system was available form Datamax, Inc. 1965 Pratt Blvd., Elk Grove Village, IL 60007.

I'll include the price list for the system in a later post here in the next few days.  In January of 1983, the complete system in the picture would have set you back about $17,000!

I get the impression that many people don't understand the how the UV-1 is related to the Astrocade.  Does anyone have any comments or questions about the UV-1 system; like for instance, why do I talk about it in this Astrocade discussion group?

Adam

Michael Matte wrote to Datamax, Inc. in the 1980s and purchased the schematics and board layouts for the system.  He has had them since that time.  Michael based his hi-res Astrocade upon the schematics, so he did put them to good use.

The largest of these UV-1 drawings are 24" x 36".  We've been trying to figure out how to get scans of them for quite awhile.  He's taking a stab at it this week.  He has been reluctant to send the original drawings, as they could get lost in the mail.  However, he's decided to photocopy them as best as he can and then send me the originals so that they may be scanned locally.  This will probably be expensive, so I will ask here for donations to get this done.  We'll figure that out in the next month or two once I see what he sends my way.

Attached is a hand-written list that Michael sent to me that gives the details for the schematics and board layouts.  This includes schematics for such neat hardware as the interface for the floppy drive and the "Winchester drive" (yes, a hard drive!).  Also included are the schematics for the video, RGB and digitizer boards, plus other UV-1R goodies.

All of this is neat, but we still don't have access to the Z-GRASS ROM for the UV-1 system.  I guess there must be some sort of operating system too, which is included on a floppy disk, I think.  I wonder if it's some variation on CP/M?  I hope that someday a UV-1 computer pops up for sale and the software can be archived-- if it has survived after all these years.

Below is an email from Michael detailing his plans for the UV-1 drawings.

Adam


----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, June 10, 2021 7:36 PM
To: Adam Trionfo
Subject: Datamax Drawings

I'm planning to work on my Datamax drawings project next week. For myself, I will visit the UPS store and break down each blueprint into four 11x17" scanned photocopies. Fortunately, the drawings don't utilize 100% of the larger 24x36" blueprints, so this scan idea will work.

Every 11x17" blueprint scanned photocopy will be labeled (by me) with:

Datamax board name
schematic (or components layout) DWG
quadrant scanned (UL, UR, BL or BR)

For example, the upper left Digitizer Board's schematic photocopy will be labeled as:

Digitizer Board
Schematic DWG
Upper Left Quadrant

There will be some photocopies with drawing overlaps. Scanned photocopies of the smaller 18 x 24" blueprints will have the most overlaps. I will add "scan align" marks on the back of the blueprints to help me get the best scans possible.

I will photocopy 2 sets of my 11x17" blueprint scans described above. I will include 1 of these sets along with the original Datamax prints which you will receive. You will then have my scanned photocopies as an optional choice for archiving the Datamax blueprints on the Bally Alley. You will likely receive the USPS priority mail package during the 4th week in June.

I'll let you know when the package is shipped. You may be only the second person to actually see this kind of historical Datamax documentation in the last 35 years. Cool!

Bye.

I've taken 600dpi scans of the pictures on the flyer and attached them here.  These are the highest quality pictures of the UV-1R system that I've seen to date.  The second picture, with the UV-1R accessories, is the first time I've seen a complete UV-1R set-up.  Oh, and for those who are wondering, the "R" in UV-1R stands for Rackmount, as this is the system that is meant to go in a rack in a production studio.

For those who may not understand what they're looking at here, the UV-R1 computer in January 1983, cost $7,695.  It used the same three Bally custom chips used in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade; it ran in hi-res mode.  The UV-1R is just the stand-along system in the first picture.  Michael Matte included a revised price list from July 17, 1984 which shows the reduced price of the UV-1 to be $2,000 only six months later!  That's quite a decrease in the price of the system!

The second picture of the UV-1, shows the system with most of its accessories.  Here's what makes up the complete DATAMAX UV-1R Zgrass Graphics System (this information is taken directly from the flyer):

Basic Configuration:

* Graphics Tablet: the electronic canvas upon which an image can be drawn. Summagrahics Bit Pad One with power supply and four-button cursor.

* Video Monitor: Panasonic CT-1350 MG

* DATAMAX UV-1R Zgrass Graphics Computer: the heart of the system, contains the Zgrass language. Z80 microprocessor, 320 x 201 pixel resolution, 256 colors with four colors displayable per screen area.

* Computer Terminal: Televideo 910

* Floppy Disk Drive: for auxiliary storage. DATAMAX DFD-1 Dual 5.25" Floppy Drive with .77 Mbyte capacity.

* DATAMAX RGB Converter: for direct RGB output.

* Joystick Hand Controller: for special input purposes.

Software Options:

* Chart Package: for easy creation of bar, pie, and line charts with the excitement of animation.

* Weather Package: to create, edit and display animated weather maps.

* Plotter Package: Software interfaces for producing hardcopy plots.

* Fonts: nine additional available.

* Zgrass Swap Module Preparation Package: documentation and software for custom expansion of the Zgrass language.

* CP/M: makes accessible the extensive library of CP/M business and word-processing software.

* Custom software designed upon request.


Hardware Options:

* Printers: Okidata Microline 82A and Epson MX-80 Plus

* Plotters: HP7220C Graphic Plotter and HIPLOT Digital Plotter DMP Series


This computer system was available form Datamax, Inc. 1965 Pratt Blvd., Elk Grove Village, IL 60007.

I'll include the price list for the system in a later post here in the next few days.  In January of 1983, the complete system in the picture would have set you back about $17,000!

I get the impression that many people don't understand the how the UV-1 is related to the Astrocade.  Does anyone have any comments or questions about the UV-1 system; like for instance, why do I talk about it in this Astrocade discussion group?

Adam

18079:
Yes, as long as you have a cable to tv fitting, and you are going to the cable/antenna connection on your TV, then it will work if the unit is OK. As I mentioned, ANY of the chips in the unit can cause black screen. If you feel comfortable, you can remove the top plastic part of the unit, and then feel around to see if something is REAL hot. The chip under the keypad will be hot as well as the regulator with the large heat sink. There is also one regulator under the keypad that gets pretty hot. The large resistor at the front will also get hot. ANY thing else should be cool enough to put your finger on. if there is something that is very hot, chances are that item is bad. If the wall transformer gets really hot, you probably have at least one shorted component.To be certain, you really should have a schematic (available here, free) and proper test equipment.If you have a volt/ohm meter, you could check the main voltaces avaiable on the DRAM chips under the keypad. If you remove the plastic holding the keypad, be VERY careful when lifting it as the wires to the keypad may be brittle. the +10V can be found on pin 40 od the DATA chip that has a heat sink, under the keypad. +5V, -5V and +15V(or it could be +12V) can all be found on any memory chip. The +5V goes to EVERY chip on the PCB! If it is lower that +4.9, you have a problem that may not be easy to find.

Some of that document is really only for the preservationist with nothing else to do (I guess?) for it is all-time-consuming; I won't be taking the advice from there, for in that direction of hardcore scanning lies madness.

Jason Scott, of archive.org, once commented on his podcast, "Jason Scott Talks His Way Out of It," that he watches the hardcore archivists who scan documents in ways which seem similar to those described on scanning.guide.  He sees them make perfect scans; they're cleaned-up and scanned at 1200dpi.  They look amazing.  Nearly undisguisable from the original.  Then these archivists burn out and they simply drop out of sight one day.  I'm in this hobby for the long haul; I've been archiving documents for twenty years.  Do my scans look like the original?  Nope.  Note even close.  Are they readable and usable?  Yup.  To me, if you want something to look as close to the original as possible, then you're actually looking for the original, not a copy.

"The UV-1R Zgrass Graphics Computer puts computer graphics capabilities into the hands of the graphic artist. The UV-1R uses advanced video game technology and the powerful Zgrass language to produce exciting video images and high-speed animation."

and, of course:

"Zgrass is a high-level, interactive computer language that was designed to meet the demands of the artist. Zgrass simplifies the creation and manipulation of graphics in real-time. In Zgrass, complex computer graphics and realtime animation sequences can be produced in minutes without advanced programming knowledge."

Ah, but you want more information?  Well, then, here ya go:

UV-1R Specifications:

- User Memory - 32K RAM, expandable to 64K for CP/M compatibility
- Screen Memory - 256K RAM, with 192K usable as solid-state disk cache
- Resolution - 320 x 201 x 2 bits
- CPU - Z80 with hardware-assisted arithmetic processing unit
- Palette - 256 colors, with four colors displayable per area
- Firmware - Zgrass-resident 32K EPROM
- Output - NTSC composite video (RS170), RGB (optional)
- Ports - Two RS232C
- Interfaces to: Graphics tablet, 5.5 Mbyte 5.25" Winchester drive, up to eight 5.25" floppy drives, printer, plotter
- Front panel connections - Headphones and four joysticks
- Sound - Three-voice synthesizer

It's cool to think about that there was a computer that used the Bally custom chips that has a hard drive, disk drives, printers, plotters and more.  Someday this system will be emulated.  Um, right?

18087:
So instead of doing a counter off of a stripped sync (from luma) use pin 15 of the DATA IC (PPU). This signal repeats every 63.5us? and can be used to blank R-Y and B-Y.
So a clock counter would be always active and reset to 0 when pin 15 is high (1).
blanking would happen at 0-X; stop at X-Y; and restart Y-0,.
The place holders of X and Y depend on the speed of the input clock and width of blank (0-X; Y-0) and distance from blank to blank(X-Y).
This picture might make what I am talking about make more sense: https://i.imgur.com/8RuQQgr.png
The count doesn't need to be particularly accurate so long as it wipes the area of R-Y and B-Y that should be blanked.

This method can certainly be used to restore blanking to the Astrocade's signals and then convert them to RGB.
This will just be a stopgap until I figure out how to interpret the signals going to/from the DATA IC in order to convert them to colors.

18100:
My audience is always myself (think of a post as a reminder to do something; in this case make a RGB mod). The other audience is modders who might stumble upon this in the future (in order to save them time if trying to make their own designs).

The general idea is that blanking of R-Y and B-Y is not happening correctly. Why they did this has something to do with interfacing with the LM1889. For creating RGB from YPbPr it doesn't really matter why they did anything so it isn't worth investigating (for me). All I have to do is count of any repeating signal such as pin 15; sync stripped off of a LM1881, etc. TLDR the timing is not "incorrect" nor did they make some sort of error AFAIK.
Anyway, we must correct the blanking so that we may interface with "corrected" signals.

It is hard for me to explain logic. Let me try:
Think of a train on a circular track. You have 3 distinct items on/around this train. A watch (clock), a flag (in this case sync), a payload (in this case blank).
Now you go let say you complete a rotation in 60 seconds; and your clock counts in 1 second increments. You reset your timer every time you pass the flag.
You are required to drop your payload continuously both 10 seconds before the flag, while passing the flag, and 10 second after the flag (any deviation is unacceptable). <<< these numbers are arbitrary btw.

So you will miss the first 10 seconds of your payload the first pass because you haven't passed the flag yet (this is fine).
You pass the flag, start your timer, and start dropping your payload; when your timer reaches 10 seconds you stop dropping your payload.
Likewise when your timer reaches 50 seconds you know you are 10 seconds away from the flag so you start dropping your payload again.
When you pass the flag you reset your timer to 0 and repeat the process.

Notice you only miss the first 10 second of the payload and then never again because the process repeats.
That is the simplified view of what needs to be done to correct blank; the code to do this is not much more complicated than the scenario described above.

This program has been stored in the BASIC area of
This routine places by actual HL location. This routine will display 11001100 on the screen as 1010. Inputs: Takes Byte in Accumulator and places on screen at HL.

I added a Bally BASIC program from 1980 called "Decode" by John Collins (Collins Computer Company). This is a type-in BASIC listing.  This hasn't been archived in any format until now.

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#Decode_John_Collins_Type-In

This program description is from a listing of programs by John Collins:

"Decode is a utility program. This program will decode information stored in memory. You enter the decimal location of memory and the binary # and the hexadecimal # for that location and the next highest location is printed out. This utility program is useful for machine language programming. It is also useful for understanding how the Bally works."

The following advertisement for "Decode" seems to only appear on page 66 of the May 1980 issue of Arcadian:

"Checkers, Chess Board, Hangman, Bowling, Bally's Alley (an adventure program) O-hello, Inspector Clue-so, Decode are the games available from John Collins, 713 Bradford Dr., Ft. Walton Beach, FL 32548, costing: $6 per program, $8 for two, $9 for three, or $10 for four, all on his tape. More data, listing Info, etc., for an SAE."

Program advertised in this manner are amongst the rarest for the system; it's always a treat to see anything by Mr. Collins; his programs were rather sophisticated for the time of their release.

Enjoy!

Adam

Last weekend my wife and I went to an exhibit called "Clearly Indigenous: Native Visions Reimagined in Glass" at the Museum of Indian Arts and Culture" in Santa Fe.  The glass art was extraordinary.  Here is a link to the exhibit:

http://www.indianartsandculture.org/upcoming-exhibitions&eventID=4727

While we were there, we wandered around the rest of the exhibits.  Since I live in New Mexico, I've seen plenty of Navajo rug designs; they're a common sight out here.  However, this time upon seeing the Navajo rugs, I was struck by how easily they could be translated into video art (either still or animated) for the Astrocade.  By design, the rugs already look like they're created to inspire low-resolution, pixel art for computers with a limited color palette.  I don't think that I'm the first one to see this, as the pictures created by the "Atari Video Music" hardware from 1977 look similar (though it's probably a case of parallel evolution):

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wle0eqBwtL8

On Monday, I requested five books on Navajo rug design from the library.  I picked them up yesterday and I read a short one (it's mostly pictures) last night.  I've attached the cover of the book to this post and I've also inserted the image in-line here:

[cid:e00f8190-1d26-4f0f-ab2d-f0f1adeedcf7]

Even the cover of the book looks like it's a perfect fit for the Astrocade doesn't it?  For example, it looks to be only about four colors.  Bally BASIC can't handle it (mostly limited to two colors, though, yes there are workarounds), but all of the expanded BASICs, like Blue Ram BASIC and Vipersoft BASIC, could create a similar design.  Of course, a machine language program running from cartridge would have no issues creating a "rug" based on Navajo-like designs.

It's rare for art to truly inspire me, but I think somehow the designs of these rugs have broken through my thick skull and touched me.

Here are some more design examples from a semi-random website that sells Navajo rugs:

https://www.navajorug.com/pages/interior-design

Also, here are a pinterest page with plenty of more designs:

https://www.pinterest.com/ccofokc/navajo-rugs/

Is it just me, or do these neat patterns seem destined to be displayed on an Astrocade's screen?

Adam

This is just a way to restore blanking to R-Y and B-Y. The end goal being an analog conversion of YPbPr to RGB. This is not the best way to do it but it may be as far as I can get for a while.

I have been researching the Astrocade patent information (the one that holes the giant schematics).
Anyway, RGB can be converted from the digital IO's of the DATA IC.

To start I can recreate hsync, vsync, csync, and blank pretty easily.

Then it looks like the 8 RAM IO's (MD0-MD7) represent 4 pixels. Every RAM is paired with another to make a single pixel. The values being 00, 01, 10, and 11.
These values just point to one of 8 color registers. I believe where it is in time compared to the "horizontal color barrier" determines 0-3 or 4-7 color registers. (I have not read what the horizontal color barrier is yet).

Background color seems to be another variable that I am not sure about.
It seems like there is 12 bits of data multiplexed through the MXD0-MDX7 bus. So 8 bits being read followed by 4 bits to represent the full 12 bits of data?
These 12 bits would set the color registers, bg resister and a lot of other things. I think I only need to be concerned with the color registers values for now...

What I am trying to ascertain is when reads are being done for setting the color register, background register, RAM reads, and anything else that might be relevant.

Anyway, I will start writing the code to make this happen but I have a lot of gaps I need to fill in.
If someone has some deeper insight and can dumb it down into a table of sorts I would appreciate it.

18117:
"The_crayon_king" was able to get a LOT of information "just" from using the Astrocade patent.  That documentation is not easy to read; it's way above my head.  There are three patents, but I think that they all share the same information.  All three patents are in this page (but I presume that "Crayon" knows this already):

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/Astrocade_Inc.html

I'm not sure if this will be helpful, but on October 30, 2018, I uploaded to Archive.org a collection of the 46 patents cited by both of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade patents 4,301,503 and 4,296,930. It's pretty neat reading/browsing the patents referenced in the Astrocade patents. Some of the referenced patents go back as far as 1958. Also, some of the patents are for systems from Atari, Magnavox's original 1972 Odyssey or even very obscure computers like the VideoBrain.

https://archive.org/details/46PatentsCitedbytheBallyArcadeandAstrocadePatents

As Ken Lill mentioned in regard to this initial post, the "Nutting Manual" can sort of simplify some of what you're talking about.  However, the manual is aimed at program game coding.  Still, it DOES hold some pretty-good overviews of the system that will certainly help anyone reading the patent.  The "Nutting Manual" is here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#NuttingManual

Yes, the colors of the two bits that make up a pixel are stored in the registers.  You can find the names of them, as they're used in the Bally on-board ROM in the Home Video Game Library Equates file, here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/HVGLIB.zip

For instance, search the file for the phrase: "; OUTPUT Ports for VIRTUAL COLOR:"

The "horizontal color barrier" is also known as the "HORizontal Color Boundary."  See the section called "Color Mapping" on page 88 of the "Nutting Manual" to understand how it works:

https://archive.org/details/SoftwareAndHardwareForTheBallyArcadeATechnicalDescriptionDaveNuttingAssociates/page/n93/mode/1up

(I hope this long link works when you read it.)

There are some other folks here who can hopefully be more helpful for you, "Crayon."

Adam

It's been quite some time since any new Astrocade tapes have showed up, but I was recently loaned two rare commercial tapes I hadn't seen before--Tiny Arcade's Tape 103 and A.R.D.'s Gamepack G1. They're both from 1982 and for AstroBASIC. I was able to successfully archive all the recordings--9 unique programs, two with a duplicate copy. This includes 4 never before archived programs--Vindicator (Tiny Arcade), Art Show (Tiny Arcade), Caterpillar (A.R.D.), and Galactic Hitchhiker (A.R.D.). It's odd to think that I'm quite likely the first person to play these in 30+ years. Thanks to Alan Schweitzer for tracking these down and to Athena for loaning them out.

Here are some notes on my experience. I'll award best game to Caterpillar, and worst game to Galactic Hitchhiker.

Tiny Arcade Tape 103

Vindicator side: Two copies on tape, no apparent differences, but not byte for byte identical. No title screen. It's a space shooter that looks a bit like Defender. Your ship automatically moves from left to right before wrapping back to the left side of the screen. You can push left or right to slow down or speed up. Push up or down to move up or down. Pull the trigger to fire a beam a short distance in front of your ship. Use the beam to take out five stationary targets, which can fire horizontally in either direction. Avoid rockets moving directly up from the ground. Once you take out all the targets, more will generate. You have five lives to score as many points as possible. I found the rockets frustrating, as they respawn once they hit you or move above your ship, so you can get hit repeatedly when trying to take out targets near the ground.

Fireworks/Art Show side.
First recording is Fireworks. No title screen. Runs automatically.
Second recording is Art Show. Enter option 1-7 to decide what to see.
[1] Computer Crochet
[2] Spirathon
[3] Jewel Box
[4] Radiation
[5] Tones I
[6] Starflakes
[7] Combined Display

Gamepack G1 has five recordings on the front.
Part 1: Micro-Pac
This is a very slow Pac-Man clone where the ghosts can pass through walls. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 2: Caterpillar
The raw recording jumps at one point. I couldn't get the first recording to process correctly, but the second recording worked with the -l2 option. It's a Centipede clone. Move left and right with the joystick and pull the trigger to shoot at the caterpillar and occasional spiders. You only fire when lined up with the spider or the head of the caterpillar. There's no up or down motion, so you lose a life if the caterpillar or spider reaches the bottom of the screen. The speed is good for BASIC, but it gets difficult to see the caterpillar through the background mushrooms as the game progresses.
Part 3: Tic-Tac-Tollah
Enter moves with keypad. Invalid entries crash program. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 4: The Paper Chase
Grab the highlighted toilet paper roll by turning the knob to aim and pulling the trigger. You compete against a computer controlled opponent. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 5: Galactic Hitchhiker
I found it difficult to figure out how to play this, an opinion shared by the review in Arcadian volume 5, issue 3. I think you use the joystick to steer around obstacles rushing toward you in a first person view. But I'm not sure what you're supposed to do when it tells you to avoid rays.

Gamepack G1 had one recording on the reverse side, which is a copy of Micro-Pac. It works fine but has extraneous text on the title screen.

Paul

The "Plain BASIC Talk" series, written by Ken Lill, originally appeared in 1982, 1983 and 1985 in the "Arcadian" newsletter for the Bally Arcade/Artocade.  This new article was written in July 2021!

The article is called "Stack Woes, When Things are STACKed Against You!"
Ken was inspired to write it as he was looking through the BASIC listing of the recently archived "Star Trek" by Scott Waldinger.

You can read Ken's new BASIC tutorial/article here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/basic.html#Plain_BASIC_Talk_Stack_Woes

If you are newish to BASIC programming with the either the Bally or Astrocade BASIC cartridges, there are a couple of things you will need to know about the STACK. This article gives you an overview of how the stack is affected when using BASIC.

Thanks for writing this new article, Ken.  I read it over and proofread it.  It features quite a few lessons that might help someone track down some issues with their short BASIC programs.

Adam

Subject: [ballyalley] Tiny Arcade Tape 103 and A.R.D. Gamepack G1 archived

It's been quite some time since any new Astrocade tapes have showed up, but I was recently loaned two rare commercial tapes I hadn't seen before--Tiny Arcade's Tape 103 and A.R.D.'s Gamepack G1. They're both from 1982 and for AstroBASIC. I was able to successfully archive all the recordings--9 unique programs, two with a duplicate copy. This includes 4 never before archived programs--Vindicator (Tiny Arcade), Art Show (Tiny Arcade), Caterpillar (A.R.D.), and Galactic Hitchhiker (A.R.D.). It's odd to think that I'm quite likely the first person to play these in 30+ years. Thanks to Alan Schweitzer for tracking these down and to Athena for loaning them out.

Here are some notes on my experience. I'll award best game to Caterpillar, and worst game to Galactic Hitchhiker.


Tiny Arcade Tape 103

Vindicator side: Two copies on tape, no apparent differences, but not byte for byte identical. No title screen. It's a space shooter that looks a bit like Defender. Your ship automatically moves from left to right before wrapping back to the left side of the screen. You can push left or right to slow down or speed up. Push up or down to move up or down. Pull the trigger to fire a beam a short distance in front of your ship. Use the beam to take out five stationary targets, which can fire horizontally in either direction. Avoid rockets moving directly up from the ground. Once you take out all the targets, more will generate. You have five lives to score as many points as possible. I found the rockets frustrating, as they respawn once they hit you or move above your ship, so you can get hit repeatedly when trying to take out targets near the ground.

Fireworks/Art Show side.
First recording is Fireworks. No title screen. Runs automatically.
Second recording is Art Show. Enter option 1-7 to decide what to see.
[1] Computer Crochet
[2] Spirathon
[3] Jewel Box
[4] Radiation
[5] Tones I
[6] Starflakes
[7] Combined Display


Gamepack G1 has five recordings on the front.
Part 1: Micro-Pac
This is a very slow Pac-Man clone where the ghosts can pass through walls. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 2: Caterpillar
The raw recording jumps at one point. I couldn't get the first recording to process correctly, but the second recording worked with the -l2 option. It's a Centipede clone. Move left and right with the joystick and pull the trigger to shoot at the caterpillar and occasional spiders. You only fire when lined up with the spider or the head of the caterpillar. There's no up or down motion, so you lose a life if the caterpillar or spider reaches the bottom of the screen. The speed is good for BASIC, but it gets difficult to see the caterpillar through the background mushrooms as the game progresses.
Part 3: Tic-Tac-Tollah
Enter moves with keypad. Invalid entries crash program. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 4: The Paper Chase
Grab the highlighted toilet paper roll by turning the knob to aim and pulling the trigger. You compete against a computer controlled opponent. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 5: Galactic Hitchhiker
I found it difficult to figure out how to play this, an opinion shared by the review in Arcadian volume 5, issue 3. I think you use the joystick to steer around obstacles rushing toward you in a first person view. But I'm not sure what you're supposed to do when it tells you to avoid rays.

Gamepack G1 had one recording on the reverse side, which is a copy of Micro-Pac. It works fine but has extraneous text on the title screen.

Paul

AFAIK,. there are 4 pairs of pixels data (regs).

When latch0 is '1' then the values are committed to the register.
So each of the 4 have a value of 00,01, 10, 11 that would point to a color value (which is held in the color register [which I haven't figured out yet]).
Anyway I would have to believe that when latch0 goes from 1 to 0 (falling edge) that the Bally steps through each of the register values in order.
So reg1 value, reg2 value.... etc.

I don't know the widths of each pixel or when in time from the latch0 pins that the registers begin their sequence.  This is stuff I can figure out later so not super important atm.

I assume at the end of the last reg the color goes to the background reg color.
So if you have fed it more pixel data from the RAM it will do that., if else it will go to the BG color.

Alot of the data out there is written from the perspective of the Z80; which is why I am making all these assumptions.

approx 34 to make hsync
using 7M as the clock source.
Then doing AND logic to sum for Csync.

18158:
As I mentioned last month, Ken Lill's "Plain BASIC Talk" series appeared in 1982, 1983, and 1985 in the "Arcadian" newsletter for the Bally Arcade/Artocade.  Last month, in July, he wrote another article.  Now he's done it again!  This new article was finished only yesterday, on August 19, 2021!

The article is called "A Remake of Scott Waldinger's "Startrek."  It gives some tips to Bally/Astro BASIC programmers for speeding up programs and some space saving techniques using Startrek as a programming example.

You can read Ken's new BASIC tutorial/article about "Star Trek" here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/basic.html#Plain_BASIC_Talk_Star_Trek_Remake

I have combined Ken's original three pdf files into one document for his latest project.  If someone wants to type in Ken's version and test it, he would appreciate finding out how it stacks up against the original.

Last month's article "Stack Woes" is here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/basic.html#Plain_BASIC_Talk_Stack_Woes

You can read most of Ken's articles from the Arcadian, including his "Plain BASIC Talk" series, here:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_misc/Arcadian_Articles/Arcadian_Articles.html#KenLill

Thanks for writing this new article, Ken.  I hope some people read it over and try it out.  It's hard to believe that Ken has jumped in and continued this series nearly 40 years after he wrote the first article; amazing!

Adam

18168:
I was getting a lot of gibberish out of tapes that Allen recently sent me, so I did a search to see if there were any alternate tools available for the 300 baud tapes using the Kansas City Standard. I found a program published fairly recently, TapeTool2 by Topten Software.

https://www.toptensoftware.com/tapetool/

After playing around with the options a bit, I got much better results for two tapes that were giving me trouble. I also like that audio filter support is built directly into the program. Both highpass and bandpass filters work well, bandpass maybe a bit better. I also found I sometimes needed to turn the noise threshold way down to make it sensitive to small signals. An example command for decoding to a binary file is:

tapetool2.exe ww6-raw.wav bandPass kansas.audioToBytes --noiseThreshold:0  ww6-bandPass-noise0.bin

Then the .bin file can be converted to a .txt file with prg2txt, or back to a good .wav file as usual.

I recently tracked down Dale Low, programmer for Astrogames. Astrogames published tape collections including games like Multi-Adventure, Defense Pro, Metro Attack, Night Bombers, Star Wahs, Wah's Revenge, and Super Pac. He kindly agreed to answer a few questions for me. You can find Dale at http://gumbypp.com/

Paul: Do you remember how you got interested in the Astrocade system? What made you take the leap from playing to game development?

Dale: I don't. I do vaguely remember being excited when Astro BASIC came out, similar to the excitement that I felt when Apple released the first iOS SDK (I'm now a professional iOS developer).

Paul: Approximately how many copies of your tapes were you able to sell?

Dale: I went through my records and think that I sold a grand total of around 50 tapes over a few years - LOL. It definitely was not a big money-making endeavor!

Paul: I've always been particularly intrigued reading about the Multi-Adventure tape. It was pretty rare to attempt platformers in BASIC, but it sounds like The Forest played kind of like Pitfall, with rope swings and leaping between small platforms. How were you able to get that working?

Dale: I have no idea :)

Paul: Was there a lot of machine language involved?

Dale: Unfortunately, I don't remember that either.

Paul: Michael Prosise's review said you should make an Extended BASIC version (for one of the RAM expansions). Did you ever consider that?

Dale: I don't think that I seriously considered that. It was harder to get stuff in Canada at the time and I was only 17 with a limited budget. But I was definitely pleased with the positive feedback in the Arcadian review.

Paul: Are there any games that stand out to you? The reviewers also liked Night Bombers, Defence Pro, and Metro Attack.

Dale: Probably Multi-Adventure. I liked the idea of a non-traditional arcade game. Being able to load multiple segments from tape worked well for this type of game given that we only had 1800 bytes to work with at the time!

Paul: I see that you went on to do a lot of other software development. Several people have mentioned that the Astrocade was what first got them interested in programming. Would you say the same?

Dale: I would. I'm actually a little disappointed that I didn't continue with independent software development after Astrogames. I just went the usual route of going to university, getting a degree (in EE) and then a "normal" job working for a regular company. That said, I have been an independent software developer since mid 2014 as a consultant, not as an indie publisher.

Paul: I unfortunately have not actually played the games I'm asking you about, because I've never found one of the tapes. Given the reviews I've read, you might say they're on the "most wanted" list of Astrocade tape games. Have you held onto any of your tapes or documentation?

Dale: I have a small folder which has the "ads" and reviews of the tapes, but that's about it. I live in San Francisco now, but there may still be stuff in my parents' basement in Victoria. I'll check the next time I go visit (which might be possible now with Covid border restrictions loosening somewhat). Even if I can find old tapes, I'm not sure that they would be loadable. I guess there's a process that some folks use to convert an audio wave file into a binary? If I find anything, I'll let you know.

Paul: Have you kept in touch with any other developers for the system?

Dale: I have not.

Paul: That's all I can think of for now. I'll pass on your responses to the mailing list and we might have a few followup questions.

Dale: Glad to help. I'm really happy to see that the Astrocade still has an active fan base.

--------------

Anything else people want to know from Dale?

Paul

18173:
Greetings all! 

 

I'm excited to be part of this group and wanted to share a quick
introduction. I've been heavily interested in 2nd generation consoles and
home computers for many years now (especially late-70s through mid-80s). The
only 2nd gen console I experienced growing up was an Atari 2600. Over time I
learned about and acquired other popular game consoles from the era
(Intellivision, Colecovision, Odyssey) but hold much more intrigue and
appreciation for the underdogs and largely forgotten systems of the day,
especially the Bally.

 

My discovery of Bally began when I was searching out podcasts built around
Z80-based architectures to listen to on long road trips. I hold a bias
toward Z80 powered machines simply because I have a lot more familiarity
with that architecture and my other most beloved obscure platform is the
Z80-based Mattel Aquarius, which only survived in the market for a few
months before being axed. My searches led to the discovery of Adam's Bally
Alley podcast and the amazing wealth of information preserved on the website
about a system that otherwise could've been largely lost to history. The
more I learned about the system the more impressed I was. I've enjoyed
listening to the podcasts and sifting through the abundance of materials
about this unique and very capable platform. It was fun to review the
origins of the Arcadian newsletter and all of the anticipation the
contributors had back then to the release of Bally BASIC-and rightfully so.
I am a computer programmer both by profession and as a hobbyist and am most
drawn to the development and technical capabilities of the Bally.

 

I imagine how incredible it must had felt to the lucky owners of the Bally
back in the day with the debut of BASIC. This was not just a gimmick "make
your own game in minutes" sort of cartridge or novelty that some platforms
had, but instead offered a full-blown implementation of BASIC complete with
save/load  capabilities via cassette (both the 300 and 2000 baud variants).
Had I grown up at the time and been treated to this sort of revolution to a
system that I initially expected was only to play games on, there's no doubt
I would've spent many months mastering the syntax and creating a lot of
programs for my own enjoyment and to share with others. The features of its
BASIC implementation are leaps and bounds more complete than other dedicated
platforms; this includes the aforementioned Aquarius, which released 5 years
later as a home computer but still lacked most things that the Bally offered
(Aquarius contained only a 80x72 drawable view, 16 colors, no GPU, a fixed
character ROM, no built-in BASIC commands to handle graphics or interface
with joysticks/multi-voice sound found on the expander).

 

With many thanks to Allen Schweitzer and his devotion toward Bally
restoration and preservation, I am now the owner of a functional physical
machine. I avoided emulating any aspects of the system until I had a
physical one to use, since I wanted my entire experience to be organic just
as it would've felt back in the day. Bally's games are highly impressive and
I am still just starting to work my way through the library. Both the
visuals and sound effects seem directly comparable to an authentic arcade
experience from that time period. The controllers are really innovative and
fun to use given the multi-purpose of the analog stick unlike anything I've
seen before. The first night I had it operating my mom visited and we both
had a blast playing the integrated Gunfight game, which was one of the first
games my mom had played since Stampede on the Atari 2600! It was tremendous
fun and we got a lot of laughs out of it.

 

Last night I played the Bally BASIC demonstration program and just watching
that and seeing the potential even just in BASIC alone was fascinating and
again I imagine how intriguing this would had been to Bally owners back in
the day, when suddenly a full programmable computer was at their fingertips
(even if the planned keyboard/PC accessories never came to fruition). I also
have dabbled into Z80 machine language for other platforms and look forward
to development efforts and experimentation with the Bally for years to come.

 

Thank you all!

 

Matt

So from my research, the Channel F was pretty well received but was really doomed by what was happening to Fairchild more broadly. Fairchild took a bath on the digital watch market when that fad ended and so produced the Channel F in pretty conservative quantities. You can find coverage in the late 70s indicating that people would buy the Channel F if they could find one, but they just couldn't snag any. Contrast to Atari, which overproduced the VCS in 1978 and took a hit to their profits that year. And of course, in the end Fairchild's struggles in other areas of business led to several rounds of layoffs before selling off their video game stuff to Zircon (and then selling the rest of the company in its entirety). So maybe the Channel F could have been more than a blip, but it would have required quite a bit to have changed with the broader company's situation.
The Channel F also suffered from the struggle to get FCC approval, and only barely made the 1976 Christmas season with like 15,000 units (and a higher price point than they'd originally planned for). They did also pioneer the idea of selling new cartridges around the year and not just at Christmas, albeit to help them offset the costs of the Channel F console itself...

I’ve been heavily interested in 2nd generation consoles and home computers for many years now (especially late-70s through mid-80s). The only 2nd gen console I experienced growing up was an Atari 2600. Over time I learned about and acquired other popular game consoles from the era (Intellivision, Colecovision, Odyssey) but hold much more intrigue and appreciation for the underdogs and largely forgotten systems of the day, especially the Bally.  My discovery of Bally began when I was searching out podcasts built around Z80-based architectures to listen to on long road trips. I hold a bias toward Z80 powered machines simply because I have a lot more familiarity with that architecture and my other most beloved obscure platform is the Z80-based Mattel Aquarius, which only survived in the market for a few months before being axed. My searches led to the discovery of Adam’s Bally Alley podcast and the amazing wealth of information preserved on the website about a system that otherwise could’ve been largely lost to history. The more I learned about the system the more impressed I was. I’ve enjoyed listening to the podcasts and sifting through the abundance of materials about this unique and very capable platform. It was fun to review the origins of the Arcadian newsletter and all of the anticipation the contributors had back then to the release of Bally BASIC—and rightfully so. I am a computer programmer both by profession and as a hobbyist and am most drawn to the development and technical capabilities of the Bally.  I imagine how incredible it must had felt to the lucky owners of the Bally back in the day with the debut of BASIC. This was not just a gimmick “make your own game in minutes” sort of cartridge or novelty that some platforms had, but instead offered a full-blown implementation of BASIC complete with save/load  capabilities via cassette (both the 300 and 2000 baud variants). Had I grown up at the time and been treated to this sort of revolution to a system that I initially expected was only to play games on, there’s no doubt I would’ve spent many months mastering the syntax and creating a lot of programs for my own enjoyment and to share with others. The features of its BASIC implementation are leaps and bounds more complete than other dedicated platforms; this includes the aforementioned Aquarius, which released 5 years later as a home computer but still lacked most things that the Bally offered (Aquarius contained only a 80x72 drawable view, 16 colors, no GPU, a fixed character ROM, no built-in BASIC commands to handle graphics or interface with joysticks/multi-voice sound found on the expander).  With many thanks to Allen Schweitzer and his devotion toward Bally restoration and preservation, I am now the owner of a functional physical machine. I avoided emulating any aspects of the system until I had a physical one to use, since I wanted my entire experience to be organic just as it would’ve felt back in the day. Bally’s games are highly impressive and I am still just starting to work my way through the library. Both the visuals and sound effects seem directly comparable to an authentic arcade experience from that time period. The controllers are really innovative and fun to use given the multi-purpose of the analog stick unlike anything I’ve seen before. The first night I had it operating my mom visited and we both had a blast playing the integrated Gunfight game, which was one of the first games my mom had played since Stampede on the Atari 2600! It was tremendous fun and we got a lot of laughs out of it.  Last night I played the Bally BASIC demonstration program and just watching that and seeing the potential even just in BASIC alone was fascinating and again I imagine how intriguing this would had been to Bally owners back in the day, when suddenly a full programmable computer was at their fingertips (even if the planned keyboard/PC accessories never came to fruition). I also have dabbled into Z80 machine language for other platforms and look forward to development efforts and experimentation with the Bally for years to come.  Thank you all!  Matt

18191:
I disagree. Having gone through the 1977 lineups of the Studio II, Channel F, and the Atari VCS... they're all pretty comparable in terms of quality and content. The controls on the Studio II are weird in hindsight but no less weird than what you'd find on dedicated machines. The big weakness is the lack of color and the lack of corporate support; the Studio II wasn't picked up by the usual RCA commercial division (which probably would have muscled its way onto the market sooner and more forcefully) but rather than paltry special products division, which dealt in like, tv antennas and the like. Much smaller budget, much less clout. 
The Studio II did well enough in its test markets early in 1977 that RCA's people felt like it was worth a broader release and that a color revision (the Studio III) could be delayed. I'm guessing that's in no small part because of limited availability of the Channel F and no competition from the VCS until around August/September. To me as someone who likes to dig into game history and look at the context behind these games and systems, both the Channel F and the Studio II - and indeed, the Bally Arcade - are unfairly maligned and overlooked. They all failed, but they all failed for specific reasons that really showcase why Atari's machine succeeded on the market... and they all are really interesting in their own ways.

I do think it all comes down to what metric you're using for success. As far as market success goes all three certainly "failed" but for all very different reasons. But the Bally has this rich legacy of fanworks owing to it having one foot in the computer market. The Channel F did well for Fairchild, hit the market first, and really set a bar for programmable game systems that immediately made them the hot item over dedicated machines. You could argue the Bally Arcade failed because Bally itself was not a consumer products company and because the price tag was chunky (and Astrocade apparently had no shortage of internal political infighting that hurt the system). The Channel F suffered from Fairchild having issues in its other markets, leading to fewer resources and more conservative production for the game system. The Studio II had little corporate backing to get it into stores and homes, and was technologically leapfrogged by the Channel F. I think these are useful contrasts to have vs the stuff that did do pretty well, like the Odyssey2 or Intellivision, and the stuff that did spectacularly like the Atari VCS.

I was getting a lot of gibberish out of tapes that Allen recently sent me, so I did a search to see if there were any alternate tools available for the 300 baud tapes using the Kansas City Standard. I found a program published fairly recently, TapeTool2 by Topten Software.

https://www.toptensoftware.com/tapetool/

After playing around with the options a bit, I got much better results for two tapes that were giving me trouble. I also like that audio filter support is built directly into the program. Both highpass and bandpass filters work well, bandpass maybe a bit better. I also found I sometimes needed to turn the noise threshold way down to make it sensitive to small signals. An example command for decoding to a binary file is:

tapetool2.exe ww6-raw.wav bandPass kansas.audioToBytes --noiseThreshold:0  ww6-bandPass-noise0.bin

Then the .bin file can be converted to a .txt file with prg2txt, or back to a good .wav file as usual.

18200:
I passed on Kevin's questions and here are the responses.

Kevin:  What did your friends and family think of the system generally and your games?

Dale: I'm sure that people thought it was a cheap knockoff of the Atari 2600. It wouldn’t surprise me if my parents got it because it was on sale :). Of course, when I first got it, I had no idea that it would be user-programmable. I actually don't recall getting any specific feedback on my games from friends and family at the time, though I'm sure that they were amused.

Kevin: Looking back, what do you think about the Bally Arcade as a game system and as a development platform?

Dale: I thought it was amazing at the time. Of course, writing programs using the small keypad with the screen constantly changing colours was challenging, but with only 1800 bytes to fill it wasn't too bad.

Kevin: What experiences, if any, did you have with arcades or games on other systems? Did anything from those serve as inspirations for anything you worked on?

Dale: I didn't have any other development experiences back then, game or otherwise; going to the arcade as a teenager was always fun and definitely inspired me to try to create my own games. After Astrogrames, I didn't really do any professional game development, but I would say that whatever inspired me to create Astrogrames in the first place "permanently" transformed me into a part-time tinkerer outside of normal work; some of my projects are shared here: https://github.com/gumbypp? tab=repositories ( https://github.com/gumbypp?tab=repositories ). More recently, I have written a few simple games for a joytstick-enabled variant of https://github.com/gumbypp/ PixArt ( https://github.com/gumbypp/PixArt ) and its successor (a 20x30 NeoPixel LED board), and also encouraged my son to do the same.

In some respects, I've come full circle as writing code in 2021 for a limited memory-constrained environment like the Arduino Uno is not unlike writing code for the Astrocde 35+ (!) years ago.

I also enjoy sharing my love of tinkering with kids. I've taught 3 middle school "Coding & Making" tech elective classes at my kids' middle school and had just started teaching the fourth when Covid shut everything down :(.

Kevin: Do you remember which of your tapes were the most popular?

I would guess Multi-Adventure, but I'm not really sure. Of course, I only sold 50-ish tapes in total, so the term “popular” is relative :)

Good find. It's interesting to see the last gasps of the Astrocade, Video
Brain, and Interact. Even with proper management, distribution, and the
rights type of software, they would have all had a hard time lasting
through 1982 anyway with the relative tsunamis of Coleco with the
ColecoVision on the console side and Commodore with the Commodore 64 on the
computer side, especially as by 1983 their respective prices began to drop
dramatically and tons of companies began to buckle under both the price
pressures and the "Crash." It's almost like they were the
vanguards/harbingers of what would eventually befall so many of the other
companies.

From my personal experience, I'd say the Interact didn't have much to
offer, while the Video Brain was slicker than it had any right to be at the
time it was released (but it goes without saying that some curious design
and release decisions kind of dulled that shine from a practical
standpoint). It would have been interesting to see what a Video Brain 2
might have entailed from those same minds. Same thing with the Astrocade.
It would have been fascinating to see what an Astrocade 2 might have
entailed and a proper computer add-on released. After all, up until roughly
1984, the expansion of a console into a full-blown computer as a would-be
smashing success was still a dream of many companies (and something we
obviously came to find was never a significant market).

Exploding components aside, I've always unplugged the power adapter on this and other consoles when not in use as a force of habit.  More so because my introduction to gaming pre-dates surge protectors, at least I don't remember any such thing being used back in the day (at least not in my house).  
I think the root of this comes from my dad's habit of unplugging things when not in use, but no idea where he got that from (the army maybe?  dunno).  That and I remember he use to unplug stuff when there was a bad storm outside, like the TV (we only had like 7 channels back then so there wasn't much to miss). 
So not wanting my stuff to get "fried" stuck with me.  Also, I know certain power adapters continue to draw a small amount of power even if what they power isn't turned on.

18222:
Merchandising was a trade magazine for retailers, particularly those who dealt with appliances, toys and home electronics. So like, ovens, washing machines, CB radios, VCRs, VideoDisc, computers, video games, digital watches, etc. The Library of Congress has most of the issues from 76-86 in some form or another so I've been making trawls through their collection every so often. Of particular note, they cover sales data and trends, which is a rarity for game systems and computers at the time. They don't tend to break it down any further than consoles (or maybe consoles and software) but it's still very useful.
Weekly Television Digest is another trade periodical that was focused on the home TV industry and related accessories, which included computers and video games.     On Wednesday, September 8, 2021, 09:59:27 PM EDT, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:

18235:
These comments about RF quality makes me feel as though I'm very far out of the loop.  For me, I expect that looking at a crystal-clear picture coming out of an Astrocade would look like the system was running under emulation.  I wouldn't say I like RF interference, but I do like that it muddles the pixels and colors a bit.  I have the s-video upgrade, but I only use it when I'm recording sound from the Astrocade.

Yet, I do get this conversation and there certainly multiple reasons to try to have the clearest picture available from the Bally Arcade system.  For instance, if you're using Bally BASIC then the RF interference can be a burden on the eyes.  It's much worse if you're trying to program in Blue Ram BASIC which has the much-smaller character set.  If you're capturing the output from an Astrocade for a video, the you also want a clear picture.

There are also drawbacks to a picture that's too clear.  I don't think that these affect the Astrocade, but if you use s-video on an Atari 8-bit system, then some games display in B&W because the system loses the ability to have color generated by taking advantage of NTSC's poor quality.  This "trick" is called artifact color, but I don't believe that the Astrocade can get color in this way.

I'm glad to see this talk about RF/composite/s-bideo being popular.  Perhaps there is someone on this group who will give another go to providing an RF alternative for those people that want it.

Adam

18236:
Yeah we each have our own approach. For the Vectrex, I'd never get rid of the audio buzz as that's part of playing a Vectrex to me, while people do sell kits to reduce or eliminate it, as there is a demand to do so. I am very much a fan of how a CRT interprets video over an LCD, for things made for CRT. Game artists took advantage of the fact that pixels weren't exactly defined and even different colors behave in different ways. This is why something that looks like a block mess on LCD can look like something with smooth details on a CRT. The space between scanlines also gets filled in by your brain and smooths it out some. If you plug a console made for CRT into a modern TV, you're really seeing unprocessed image data, meant to be run through a CRT to achieve the desired final appearance.
That said, I do like to provide my CRT with the clearest image I can in most cases. I only find it looking like an emulator if I run it to an LCD or other modern set. The twitter account @crtpixels has some great side-by-side comparisons of pixel art and how it looks better (or at least as intended) on a CRT.
I'm not saying everyone should play like I do. If you're enjoying Astrocade on a Pi, you're still giving it more love than most, and games should be about having fun. Achieve that however you like. I'm a bit of a hardware enthusiast and CRT purist, but won't fault anyone else for playing how they like.
But yeah, give us some Astrocade options, anyone who is smart enough and listening! :)

Yeah we each have our own approach. For the Vectrex, I'd never get rid of the audio buzz as that's part of playing a Vectrex to me, while people do sell kits to reduce or eliminate it, as there is a demand to do so. I am very much a fan of how a CRT interprets video over an LCD, for things made for CRT. Game artists took advantage of the fact that pixels weren't exactly defined and even different colors behave in different ways. This is why something that looks like a block mess on LCD can look like something with smooth details on a CRT. The space between scanlines also gets filled in by your brain and smooths it out some. If you plug a console made for CRT into a modern TV, you're really seeing unprocessed image data, meant to be run through a CRT to achieve the desired final appearance.

That said, I do like to provide my CRT with the clearest image I can in most cases. I only find it looking like an emulator if I run it to an LCD or other modern set. The twitter account @crtpixels has some great side-by-side comparisons of pixel art and how it looks better (or at least as intended) on a CRT.

I'm not saying everyone should play like I do. If you're enjoying Astrocade on a Pi, you're still giving it more love than most, and games should be about having fun. Achieve that however you like. I'm a bit of a hardware enthusiast and CRT purist, but won't fault anyone else for playing how they like.

But yeah, give us some Astrocade options, anyone who is smart enough and listening! :)

Yet, I do get this conversation and there certainly multiple reasons to try to have the clearest picture available from the Bally Arcade system.  For instance, if you're using Bally BASIC then the RF interference can be a burden on the eyes.  It's much worse if you're trying to program in Blue Ram BASIC which has the much-smaller character set.  If you're capturing the output from an Astrocade for a video, the you also want a clear picture.

There are also drawbacks to a picture that's too clear.  I don't think that these affect the Astrocade, but if you use s-video on an Atari 8-bit system, then some games display in B&W because the system loses the ability to have color generated by taking advantage of NTSC's poor quality.  This "trick" is called artifact color, but I don't believe that the Astrocade can get color in this way.

I'm glad to see this talk about RF/composite/s-bideo being popular.  Perhaps there is someone on this group who will give another go to providing an RF alternative for those people that want it.

18247:
I can remember having a TV when I was knee high to a grasshopper. I was born in 1947. One set we had had a note on the back stating it was compatible with a color wheel. Imagine being able to watch a color TV in the early '50s! Look up what a color wheel was for TVs. The concept was brilliant at the time!

    On Thursday, September 9, 2021, 05:31:32 PM EDT, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:  
 
 I miss my Commodore 1084S monitor.  It burned-up (literally) over a decade ago.  It's always nice to hear from people who admire the Commodore monitors.  In the 1990s, I used to use a Commodore 1702 monitor with my first DVD player.  The quality of the picture amazed me at the time.

This past weekend, I used my Commodore Amiga-label monitor (model 1080) with an Atari 800XL that is only displaying a B&W signal; which I thought meant it was PAL, but I guess not (I guess the color is just missing due to a hardware error).  This Commodore Amiga monitor was made in 1986 and it's still going strong.  I keep it around mainly because it supports both NTSC and PAL signals, which is helpful when playing Amiga games.

I do wonder what will happen when all the CRT TVs die; but that's really a silly problem for me to worry about at all, as, surely, they will outlast me by decades.

This conversation does remind me that I saw a TV from the 1940s at a local art museum this summer.  I looked the model up while I was there and I think it was made in something like 1947, but I can't be certain.  That TV didn't work; it was a hollow hulk used in an art display, but it did make me think, "Damn, television has been around a LONG time!"

I understand that videogame consoles required late-1960s/early 1970s electronics technology to be invented before a videogame system could be made, but I'd love to see an Atari 2600 or Astrocade being played on a B&W, 1950s model television.  The oldest TV that I have is a B&W, 5" portable TV from 1976.  It's a bit too small for videogame uses, but I keep it around because, one, I got it for just $5 a few years ago and, two, it's neat to play Pong on it.

Adam
